A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same XFactor study. Text, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–B are readable, allowing retained, relocated, and newly added material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original transferability, pose-probing, ablation, and reconstruction experiments across four datasets in Tables 1–4.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds objective comparisons, robustness tests, perceptual evaluations, and qualitative analyses in Appendix B.

M1.justification: The stereo-monocular model, transferability objective, pose-preserving augmentation, and multi-view fine-tuning remain unchanged. The loss and masking descriptions move into Section 3.5. Augmented inference and corrupted training are additional experimental interventions, not revisions to the default method.

E1.justification: Both versions use RE10K, DL3DV, MVImgNet, and CO3Dv2. Appendix B adds visually corrupted-video oracle tests and masked-input transfer evaluation, extending evaluated input conditions without adding datasets or domains.

E2.justification: RayZer and RUST remain the main NVS comparators. Table 6 adds trained SimCLR and VICReg objective baselines, Figure 3 adds LVSM as a qualitative artifact comparator, and Tables 8–9 evaluate COLMAP as an alternative TPS oracle. Less3Depend is newly discussed but not benchmarked.

E3.justification: The main evaluation retains 4,000 sequence pairs per dataset and five target frames. New experiments introduce pose swapping between augmented sequences, encoder-only SSL training, probabilistic mixtures of one- and two-frame temporal offsets, and oracle evaluation under visual corruption with registration success reporting. These substantially extend experimental procedures.

E4.justification: Appendix B adds tests of whether rendering-based training outperforms standard SSL objectives, robustness to imperfect pose correspondence, TPS oracle sensitivity and registration failures, masked-transfer fidelity, and LVSM reconstruction artifacts. These investigate several methodological and evaluation weaknesses beyond the retained design ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. The added tables retain point-estimate reporting; VICReg's batch variance and covariance describe its training objective, not uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Every numerical entry in Tables 1–4 is unchanged. Tables 5–9 add substantial results under new experimental conditions. For example, Table 6 reports RE10K probe AUC at 20 degrees of 54.8 for XFactor versus 3.8 for SimCLR and 0.8 for VICReg; Table 8 reports 100% VGGT registration success versus 21.4–52.3% for COLMAP across datasets.

T1.justification: Equations 1–12, including the transferability definition, TPS metric, and training objective, remain unchanged. Explicitly discussing single-scene oracle models clarifies the existing formulation without adding mathematical assumptions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, five stated contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims about transferability, geometry-free self-supervision, XFactor, and its advantage over prior models. The new geometry-free footnote clarifies terminology, while the appendix additions supply supporting evidence.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations concerning rendering's role in learning geometry, sensitivity to imperfect pose correspondence, and the reliability of TPS oracles. It qualifies masked-transfer comparisons, explains RayZer reproduction discrepancies, and uses LVSM artifacts to support the existing rendering limitation. Its assertion that corrupted variants outperform all earlier ablations is not consistently supported by Tables 3 and 7.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the 5% probability of omitting masks and AdamW weight decay of 0.005; neither establishes a changed setting. It also documents new experiments' temporal-mixing probabilities and SSL implementation choices, including InfoNCE temperature 0.1. Existing architecture, hardware, training budgets, and project access information remain.

R1.justification: Related work expands to additional explicit-3D approaches and Less3Depend, while new experiments and discussion cite SimCLR, VICReg, and camera-controlled generative models. These broaden contextual coverage without changing the central research positioning. Duplicate publication entries for existing works do not constitute new research coverage.

P1.justification: Most prose and the section hierarchy are retained. Loss and masking explanations move from the appendices into Section 3.5; terminology, grammar, author information, acknowledgments, and publication headers receive limited edits. Appendix B gains subsections, rather than the paper undergoing extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: v2 adds five tables and two figures, including oracle-corruption trajectory panels and LVSM reconstruction grids, substantially expanding visual reporting. The original illustrations and Tables 1–4 retain their content and display structure, with surrounding text reflow and a small caption correction.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens evidence for two central elements that v1 left less tested: the learning objective and the oracle underlying TPS comparisons. Tables 6–9 add alternative-objective comparisons, correspondence-corruption tests, and direct oracle robustness checks; Table 5 adds a qualified fidelity evaluation. Reproducibility also improves. The robustness discussion overstates superiority—for example, shifted DL3DV AUC is 36.2 versus the earlier bottleneck's 41.4—but this local weakness does not outweigh the substantial validation gains.
